bodyOriginal.text: Researchers here run a much larger than usual mouse study to show a ~10% slowing of aging, depending on how one slices the data, in mice genetically engineered to exhibit a growth hormone mutation that changes the interaction of circulating growth hormone with the growth hormone receptor on cell surfaces. Growth hormone is switched from a receptor agonist (binds with and activates the receptor ) to a receptor antagonist (binds with the receptor without activating it, blocking other molecules from activating it). This extension of life is entirely expected given all of the long-lived mouse lineages in which growth hormone metabolism is in some way sabotaged . This specific form of sabotage had not been tested rigorously, however. While interesting, it is worth noting that humans with Laron syndrome , an inherited dysfunction of growth hormone metabolism analogous to many of the mouse models exhibiting longevity, do not appear to live meaningfully longer than the rest of the human population.

Interventions that disrupt growth hormone (GH) action are recognized as some of the most potent methods for extending lifespan. Accordingly, GH receptor antagonists (GHA) represent potential therapeutics to improve healthspan . Somavert ( Pegvisomant for injection), used for treating patients with acromegaly , is currently the only FDA approved GHA. This drug was based on our laboratory's early 1990s discovery that mutating a codon for a conserved glycine - at position 119 in bovine GH or 120 in human GH - to a variety of amino acids , including lysine , ultimately converted GH from an agonist to antagonist. Since Pegvisomant has poor affinity to rodent GHR, it has not been tested for its ability to extend lifespan in rodents.

To address this gap, we evaluated survival in GHA transgenic mice, a mouse line that played a crucial role in the discovery and development of Pegvisomant and has been maintained in our lab since 1991. While a prior study with several limitations failed to detect lifespan extension in GHA mice, our current study addressing these limitations shows that both median and maximal lifespan were significantly increased in male and female GHA mice, with maximal lifespan extended by 186 and 265 days, respectively. Analysis of an independent cohort of 2-year-old mice revealed that GHA males and females were less frail with enhanced grip strength despite increased adiposity . These findings demonstrate for the first time that GH antagonism can improve health and extend lifespan.

articles.titleOriginal: We Are Pi's ads for Interrail break free from travel cliches to show how passengers really feel
articles.summaryOriginal: This clever poster turns a sentence into a train journey: a simple but effective design trick, delivered in style. Let's be honest, we all know what a travel ad looks like. Beautiful scenery, with not...

bodyOriginal.text: This clever poster turns a sentence into a train journey: a simple but effective design trick, delivered in style.

Let's be honest, we all know what a travel ad looks like. Beautiful scenery, with not a bulldozer or screaming infant in sight? Check. Catchy yet ultimately bland and empty slogan? Check? Smiling, impossibly attractive people? Check.

Of course, there's nothing wrong with that. Holidays for most of us are just a welcome break from everyday life, and a little bit of fantasy never did anyone any harm. And I've got nothing personally against impossibly attractive people; some of my best friends count among their number.

But if you're trying to sell consumers on something they wouldn't normally do, and in fact might be nervous of doing in a foreign country where they don't speak the lingo, you'll need to work a little harder.

That's exactly the challenge that the global brand consultancy We Are Pi , working with social agency Butterfly Effect , were presented with. They were approached by Interrail B.V, the Dutch company behind the European rail travel scheme that makes it cheap and easy to travel across the continent with a special pass.

As well as boosting the scheme, there was also a bit of brand housekeeping to do. Up until this point, Interrail B.V. had two brands for essentially the same rail pass: Interrail for people living in Europe, Eurail for visitors from elsewhere. The latter needed to be folded into the Interrail brand, following the business changing its name from Eurail B.V. to Interrail B.V. earlier in the year.

Better than flying The campaign indirectly challenges the notion that because flying is quicker, it's better. Instead, it leans into the idea that the longer journey isn't an inconvenience; it's part of the adventure, via a brand concept they've dubbed The Interrail Effect.

This was backed up by a customer survey in which around 70% of Interrail customers said their trip changed how they see the world. A similar number considered the experiences more impactful than other types of travel, and around a quarter considered it much more impactful than other holidays they'd taken.

bodyOriginal.alt: Yellow train route with text labels forming the phrase "Realising the best bit is between here and there and there" overlaid on a map of Europe for Interrail campaign

bodyOriginal.text: To get this across visually, the launch poster shows a stylised map of Europe. Running across it is a single yellow line representing a train route; only the stops aren't cities – they're words. Joining them together gives you the sentence: "Realising the best bit is between here and there."
It's a common design trick, but it works because it forces the reader to make a bit of an effort. Had the sentence been instantly legible, it wouldn't make half as much impact.

There's a nice extra touch too: the journey doesn't end with the last word; the line continues, albeit it's now dotted and straight. It's a subtle way to evoke the idea of exploring and making it up as you go along, without beating people over the head with the idea.

Creator-led campaign Another element of the campaign is a series of short video clips made by 30 creators from the US, Canada, Australia and Europe, who were asked to travel across the continent with Interrail over summer and share their experiences.

These clips sit in a comfortable space between standard YouTube shorts and glossy, cinematic films. The former would have been a bit "So what?", the second would have seemed a bit overblown for a target audience that's likely to be sleeping in the cheapest hostel. The sweet spot they've reached feels, in the words of Goldilocks, just right.
Ultimately, there's nothing particularly new in this campaign, but at the same time, there didn't need to be.

As Özlem Birkalan, chief brand and commercial officer at Interrail, puts it: "'The Interrail Effect' isn't something we invented. It's something travellers have described to us for decades, in their own words, after every journey. What's changing is that we're finally building the brand around it. Not around where people travel, but around what travelling like this does to them."

The campaign launched globally on 10 September in the UK, Australia and the US, and will roll out across a mix of paid, owned and earned channels including paid media, organic social, EDM, partnerships and PR as well as participating creators' own Instagram, TikTok and other social platforms.

articles.titleOriginal: Pentagram's twin logos for Doha Design District are a masterclass in crafting sub-brands
articles.summaryOriginal: Led by Samar Maakaroun, these two identities for a maker space and event space highlight how strong brand architecture is built on discipline, not decoration. Msheireb Downtown Doha is a planned city...

bodyOriginal.text: Led by Samar Maakaroun, these two identities for a maker space and event space highlight how strong brand architecture is built on discipline, not decoration.

Msheireb Downtown Doha is a planned city in Doha, the capital of Qatar, that's designed to regenerate the historical district of Mushayrib (literally, 'a place to drink water' in Arabic). It's been promoted as being the world's first sustainable downtown regeneration project, and one of the smartest cities on Earth. And Doha Design District (DDD) is its hub for design, innovation, and collaboration.

Director Dana Kazic approached Samar Maakaroun and her team at Pentagram with a challenge: introduce two distinct spaces within the district, while strengthening, rather than fragmenting, the parent brand.

One would be a maker's space dedicated to experimentation and artistic development; the other, an event space that becomes a destination for exhibitions, events, and public engagement. They'd be positioned physically opposite each other.

Striving for connection It sounds like either a massive challenge or the stuff of nightmares, depending on how much experience you've had dealing with having to juggle the competing demands of brands and sub-brands, not to mention different languages.

In these scenarios, the client typically wants the two sub-brand spaces to feel connected. But in practice, they often get two names that share a typeface and a colour palette, but not much else. The connection is clearly expressed in a brand guideline PDF, yet never really translates to what the public actually sees and feels.

bodyOriginal.alt: Pentagram's dual logos for Doha Design District showing Sada in orange and Mada in turquoise, split typographically down the middle
Black carrier bag with orange handles and Sada branding, displayed on a white surface in studio lighting
Mada storefront with turquoise signage and logo on white and black facade, with a blurred figure walking past

bodyOriginal.text: To avoid that scenario, Samar—whose identity for The Mosaic Rooms in London we covered back in April—and her team took the time to get things right. As they put it: "The relationship had to allow equity to move in all directions: from DDD to the sub-brands, between the sub-brands themselves, between languages, and back again into the wider district."

Naming and letter design Next up came the naming process. The team explored a range of ideas, from letter repetitions connected to the DDD symbol to Arabic words that had a spatial dimension and were easy to say out loud. The main thing was that the names needed to work together naturally and feel like two halves of a whole.

They found the solution in a pair of Arabic words that already had a relationship with each other. Mada, meaning range, reach or possibility, was chosen for the maker's space. Sada, meaning echo, was chosen for the space where finished work meets an audience.

bodyOriginal.alt: Four illuminated turquoise and black signage panels for Doha Design District displaying the mada maker space and event space branding on a white wall

bodyOriginal.text: From a visual point of view, "sada" and "mada" are built from almost identical letterforms, mirrored and rearranged, rather than drawn from scratch as two separate typefaces. Or to put it another way, one looks like the echo of another. This means the relationship between the two spaces doesn't need to be hammered home: it's immediately, instinctively obvious.

At a deeper level, there's a sense of culture and history baked into their DNA. Both names carry the letter D, which has been lifted from the existing Doha Design District symbol, while the other letterforms are inspired by the architecture of Msheireb, the downtown Doha district the whole scheme sits within.

Again, this works elegantly in making the whole brand architecture work harmoniously together. Every curve and notch in the wordmarks echoes something structural in the area, making them feel like a natural part of their surroundings, rather than something tagged on.

Key takeaway Here's what I think anyone working on a sub-brand can learn from this. It's terribly easy, especially when you're on a tight deadline, to go with the obvious solutions to making multiple brands work together. Use the same typeface, the same colour, the same grid system. And bosh! You have a unified system. Well, kinda.

bodyOriginal.alt: Neon green pixelated text and geometric shapes displayed on a black screen with cyan border, installed in a minimalist corridor with warm-lit alcoves on either side

bodyOriginal.text: This approach might look good in a presentation, but in the real world, where your designs are having to live, breathe and do their work, they run the risk of looking like an afterthought, stapled on to the parent brand rather than being an organic part of it.

What Pentagram did here was different. Rather than seeing the existing brand at surface level—the type, the colours—they delved deep into its ethos instead, and located the connective tissue that would make the new sub-brands feel naturally part of it.
The result? No one has to stand there explaining that Sada and Mada are part of the Doha Design District. It's just obvious. And that's the job.

articles.titleOriginal: Lung Fibrosis Drug Lowers Biological Age Estimates
articles.summaryOriginal: Six different aging clocks detected younger blood protein profiles in patients taking the experimental lung-fibrosis drug rentosertib. This suggests possible anti-aging effects, but separating those from the […]

bodyOriginal.text: Six different aging clocks detected younger blood protein profiles in patients taking the experimental lung-fibrosis drug rentosertib. This suggests possible anti-aging effects, but separating those from the narrower benefits of treating fibrosis remains a challenge [1].

The AI-developed drug Many drugs developed for particular diseases act on aging-related biological processes. That creates an opportunity: a clinical trial could investigate both whether a drug treats its intended disease and whether it has broader effects on aging. Ordinary clinical measurements cannot establish those broader effects, but we now have biological age clocks that closely track chronological age or predict mortality risk [2]. These clocks have been used in numerous trials as proxies to estimate the intervention’s effect on aging.

In a new study published in Nature Biotechnology , the researchers analyzed blood samples from a Phase 2a trial whose results were published last year [3]. That 12-week, randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial tested rentosertib, an inhibitor of the kinase TNIK, which has been implicated in several aging-related processes [4].

Rentosertib was developed by the longevity biotech company Insilico, using a proprietary AI-based drug discovery platform, to treat idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis (IPF), a progressive disease in which excessive scar tissue compromises lung function. IPF is age-related, with a mean age of onset around 65 years, and aging processes such as cellular senescence and inflammation are heavily involved.
The new analysis included 42 of the trial’s 71 participants. Alongside placebo, the trial tested three regimens: 30 milligrams once daily, 30 milligrams twice daily, and 60 milligrams once daily.

Lower biological age readings The researchers used six different proteomic clocks, which analyze protein levels in blood. The proteomic clocks’ appeal is partly interpretability: researchers can identify which proteins affect the readings and connect them to known biological processes more directly than is often possible with methylation-based clocks. The clocks were developed by different teams, using data from UK Biobank, including one clock developed by Insilico itself. Four of the clocks were trained on chronological age, and two on mortality.

All six clocks detected lower predicted biological ages in patients taking rentosertib, although not at every dose or visit. After four weeks, the four chronological age-based clocks rated patients taking 60 milligrams once daily (the single-dose regimen) roughly three years younger, on average, than at the start of treatment. These changes were statistically significant compared with placebo. However, the two clocks trained to predict mortality risk did not show a significant change at that dose at week four.

Patients taking 30 milligrams twice daily (the split-dose regimen) showed the most consistent decreases across both types of clocks. The largest reductions in predicted biological age appeared by week four, with little additional change over the remaining eight weeks.

These results essentially mean that patients’ blood protein profiles became more similar to those associated with younger people. They do not, however, establish that the treated patients regained years of youth or would live longer.

Is there a broad anti-aging effect? Looking beyond the clock readings, the researchers found that treatment changed the levels of 326 blood proteins, including proteins involved in fibrosis, metabolism, and cellular stress responses. Most changes in the two higher-dose groups persisted throughout the trial or appeared later in treatment, suggesting that the drug continued affecting patients’ biology even after predicted ages plateaued.

The researchers then examined which proteins contributed most to the younger age estimates. A fibrosis-associated protein, LTBP2, stood out as a major contributor. It was used by all six clocks, which raises the question of whether their agreement mainly reflects the drug’s effect on fibrosis, rather than broader slowing of aging.

To explore whether the lower age estimates reflected more than improvement in fibrosis, the researchers compared changes in predicted age with changes in lung function. The two did not closely track each other. This suggests that improved lung function alone might not explain the clock changes, although lung function does not capture every aspect of IPF.

The team then compared the treatment-induced protein changes with differences between younger and older participants in UK Biobank. With the split dose, proteins associated with aging tended to move in the opposite direction: those found at higher levels in older people tended to decrease, and vice versa. This pattern was not statistically significant with the single daily dose.

Finally, the researchers examined proteins associated with cellular senescence. These proteins tended to increase in the placebo group but decrease with treatment, suggesting that rentosertib might reduce senescence-associated activity, although the researchers did not directly measure senescent cells in tissues.

These findings strengthen the case for investigating rentosertib as a potential geroprotector. However, because fibrosis, metabolism, and senescence are closely connected, they still cannot definitively establish whether the drug affects aging beyond its benefits for IPF.

“This study illustrates how biomarkers of aging can be incorporated into conventional clinical trials,” Vadim Gladyshev, a professor of medicine at Harvard Medical School and a coauthor of the study, told Lifespan News. “If validated more broadly, such approaches could allow us to learn not only whether a treatment affects a particular disease, but also whether it influences some aspects of aging biology.”

articles.titleOriginal: Genflow’s gene therapy lowers biological age markers in aged dogs
articles.summaryOriginal: A SIRT6 gene therapy trial in senior beagles hit its primary endpoint, lowering biological age and offering a test bed for human medicine. Old dogs make surprisingly good stand-ins for aging humans. They live in our homes, eat roughly what we eat, breathe the same air and develop many of the same age-related conditions we […] The post Genflow’s gene therapy lowers biological age markers in aged do

bodyOriginal.text: A SIRT6 gene therapy trial in senior beagles hit its primary endpoint, lowering biological age and offering a test bed for human medicine.

Old dogs make surprisingly good stand-ins for aging humans. They live in our homes, eat roughly what we eat, breathe the same air and develop many of the same age-related conditions we do, just on a faster timeline. That’s part of why a UK biotech’s just-announced results from a beagle trial are getting attention well beyond the veterinary world.

Genflow Biosciences announced that its SLAB clinical trial, short for Sarcopenia and Longevity in Aged Beagles, has met its primary endpoint. The study tested the company’s SIRT6 centenarian gene therapy in dogs over the age of 10, and the treated animals showed a clear reduction in biological age compared with untreated controls, as measured by the GRIM DNA methylation clock, one of the more established tools researchers use to estimate how “old” tissue actually behaves, independent of a subject’s birthdate [ 1 ].
Borrowing biology from people who live past 100

Genflow’s approach centers on a specific variant of the SIRT6 gene, a version found more often in centenarians than in the general population, that appears to help protect cells against age-related decline. The company’s lead compound, GF-1002, delivers this centenarian variant directly, aiming to nudge aging tissue back toward a younger functional state rather than simply managing symptoms.

The trial itself was randomized and blinded, splitting 24 beagles over age 10 into four groups: two cohorts receiving naked DNA treatment at different doses, one group getting a single dose delivered via an AAV8 viral vector, and a saline control group. Hitting the primary endpoint builds on earlier signals the company had already flagged, including positive interim muscle data reported back in February and confirmation of sustained safety and efficacy at a three-month follow-up in April.

Beyond the headline result, Genflow says treated dogs showed improvement across several secondary functional and observable measures, too, though the company is holding the detailed breakdown for the Animal Longevity Summit (ALOS) in Toronto on 1–2 October. It’s a notable venue choice: ALOS bills itself as the first conference built entirely around animal longevity, and its speaker list, including researchers like Matt Kaeberlein, Vera Gorbunova and Aubrey de Grey, reads like a who’s who of the broader anti-aging research world. That overlap isn’t a coincidence. Companion animal trials are increasingly seen as a faster, more naturalistic proving ground for interventions that could eventually make their way to humans.

“Meeting the primary endpoint in SLAB is a defining milestone for Genflow,” said Dr Eric Leire, the company’s CEO. “We set out to demonstrate that our centenarian SIRT6 naked DNA therapy could measurably address age-related decline in a real-world aging mode. This provides a powerful foundation for our partner discussions across animal health. We look forward to sharing the full dataset, including the critical methylation clock and muscle histology results, with the scientific and investment communities at the Animal Longevity Summit in October.”
Dr Eric Leire, founder and CEO of Genflow Biosciences

That mention of partner discussions is worth noting. Genflow says it’s in active conversations with major global animal health companies about licensing and commercialization, which would be the fastest realistic route to market for a therapy like this: getting it into veterinary use for aging pets before the much longer road toward human regulatory approval.

Founded in 2020 and headquartered in the UK with R&D operations in Belgium, Genflow has built its pipeline entirely around age-related disease. Beyond the SIRT6 program in dogs, the company is exploring GF-1002 as a potential treatment for MASH, a common and stubborn form of liver disease, and developing a separate mRNA-based SIRT6 therapy, GF-1006, aimed at corneal disease and glaucoma.

Dogs won’t tell us everything about how a therapy like this behaves in people, and a successful trial in beagles is several steps removed from anything a human patient could access. However, sarcopenia, the muscle loss that comes with age, is one of the more universal and disabling parts of getting older, in dogs and people alike. A therapy that measurably slows it, even in a 24-dog trial, is the kind of early proof point the longevity field has been short on.

articles.titleOriginal: SCI model takes longevity beyond the clinic
articles.summaryOriginal: APLMS will use Singapore, China and India to test how longevity science can translate into function, prevention and healthier lives at scale. The Asia-Pacific Longevity Medicine Society (APLMS) is developing a regional model intended to move healthy longevity out of specialist settings and into everyday life, using Singapore, China and India as distinct environments in […] The post SCI model takes

bodyOriginal.text: APLMS will use Singapore, China and India to test how longevity science can translate into function, prevention and healthier lives at scale.

The Asia-Pacific Longevity Medicine Society (APLMS) is developing a regional model intended to move healthy longevity out of specialist settings and into everyday life, using Singapore, China and India as distinct environments in which to generate real-world evidence and test approaches to prevention. Its scope is substantial: the three countries together represent approximately 2.8 billion people – more than a third of the world’s population – but population size is only part of the proposition.

Hong Kong hosts the model’s public debut: APLMS will introduce and further develop SCI at the 2026 Asia-Pacific Healthy Longevity International Summit , running 1–4 October. The questions on the table are deceptively simple – what travels across cultures and healthcare systems, what needs reinventing locally, and whether any of this actually changes outcomes once it leaves the laboratory or the specialist clinic.

Longevity.Technology: Longevity medicine has become increasingly sophisticated at measuring aging; the more important test is whether those measurements translate into lives with more function, independence and resilience – and fewer years constrained by chronic disease. A biomarker can tell us something fascinating about aging biology; it cannot carry the shopping upstairs. The SCI model’s emphasis on real-world evidence across very different populations is therefore interesting, particularly because it treats technology as a means rather than the endpoint. Longevity medicine that stays confined to the premium clinic is, in the end, a hobby for the wealthy rather than a population-health strategy; its useful interventions have to find their way into ordinary healthcare, workplaces and communities, or they don’t much matter. That journey looks different in Singapore, China and India, and assuming otherwise – that what works in one population will travel neatly to another – is precisely the kind of assumption SCI is built to test rather than indulge. The arithmetic alone should focus the mind: at a scale of some 2.8 billion people, even a modest gain in functional health stops being modest. The interesting question is whether they can be demonstrated – then delivered.

The thinking owes something to blue zones – those pockets of the world where people seem to age unusually well. What’s striking about many of them, on APLMS’s account, is the absence of anything exceptional: no particular wealth, no advanced healthcare, just ordinary people living ordinary lives amid strong daily habits, social bonds and cultural continuity that happen to compound rather well over decades. Whether that pattern generalizes is precisely the question SCI intends to test, rather than assume.

APLMS has selected Singapore, China and India precisely because they are not interchangeable. Singapore combines established public-health infrastructure and population-based healthcare with research in geroscience and precision medicine; its multicultural population and emphasis on prevention offer one environment in which longevity approaches can be evaluated in practice.

China – the world’s second-largest economy, home to more than 1.4 billion people – brings scale of a different order, alongside growing digital-health capabilities and extensive experience in population health. Its healthcare landscape also encompasses both modern medicine and longstanding culturally rooted health practices, providing another test of what translation means when scientific evidence meets existing behaviors and systems of care.

India, now the world’s most populous country, adds considerable heterogeneity in diet, culture, family structures and community life. APLMS also points to Ayurveda and its emphasis on daily routines, nutrition, sleep, physical activity and mental wellbeing; these traditions will sit alongside India’s developing scientific, healthcare and digital-health capabilities within the proposed model.

The intention is not to identify a single cultural recipe for longevity. Quite the reverse: SCI is conceived as an evidence-led translation network capable of separating principles that prove transferable from those that remain stubbornly local.

Central to the model is a shift in emphasis from surrogate measures toward function. Aging biology and biomarkers remain important, as do digital tools and emerging interventions; APLMS argues, however, that their value should ultimately be judged against mobility, independence, chronic disease burden, wellbeing and disability-free years.

That distinction matters. Longevity research increasingly has access to exquisitely granular measurements of biological processes, yet a statistically interesting movement in a biomarker does not automatically confer a clinically meaningful benefit. Function is messier. It is also difficult to ignore.

SCI will therefore look beyond what happens during a clinical encounter to the conditions accumulated over decades – diet and movement, certainly, but also social connection, environment, purpose, community participation and access to preventive care. Medicine and technology are positioned as tools for understanding, measuring and strengthening those foundations rather than substitutes for them.

The real-world evidence component is where the model becomes more ambitious. Controlled studies remain essential for establishing efficacy and safety, but population health has an inconvenient habit of taking place under uncontrolled conditions – among different diets, healthcare infrastructures, socioeconomic circumstances and cultural expectations.

APLMS plans to establish an SCI Healthy Longevity Real-World Evidence and Translation Network, with initial work during 2026–27 expected to include a shared framework and pragmatic common outcomes, alongside opportunities for real-world studies, clinician education and implementation pathways.

A dedicated session at the Hong Kong summit – titled The SCI Healthy Longevity Model: Everyday Life, Real-World Evidence and Prevention at Scale – will begin that process, bringing together researchers, clinicians, healthcare leaders and implementation partners. The challenge will be to preserve enough methodological consistency to make findings useful while allowing sufficient local flexibility to make them relevant – scale without context is not quite scale.

Perhaps the larger proposition is where SCI ultimately intends its findings to go. APLMS explicitly envisages pathways beyond premium longevity clinics and wellness services, extending evidence-based approaches into communities, workplaces, employers, insurers and established health systems.

That is a considerably tougher translational problem than offering another test or intervention to an already engaged longevity consumer. Prevention at population level must contend with accessibility, adherence, cultural acceptability and healthcare economics; what is biologically plausible must also become practically usable.

APLMS President Dr Tim Shi frames the ambition in much the same terms. The model, he said, is not intended to create another theoretical framework or search for a single formula for aging; its purpose is “to build a practical, culturally relevant, scientifically credible and scalable model, validated through real-world evidence and translated into better prevention, healthier everyday living and ultimately better health outcomes.”
Asia-Pacific, in that sense, offers an unusually large arena in which to attempt that work – diverse, rapidly aging and far too heterogeneous for easy answers.

If SCI develops as intended, its value may lie less in producing another definition of healthy longevity than in discovering which ideas remain useful when exposed to billions of complicated, ordinary lives. That is where prevention has to work eventually.
The 2026 Asia-Pacific Healthy Longevity International Summit is 1–4 October 2026 at The Hopewell Hotel in Hong Kong – to find out more CLICK HERE .

articles.titleKo: SCI 모델은 임상을 넘어 롱제비티를 가져갑니다
articles.summaryKo: APLMS는 싱가포르, 중국, 인도를 활용해 롱제비티 과학이 기능, 예방, 그리고 대규모 건강한 삶으로 어떻게 전환될 수 있는지 시험할 예정입니다. 아시아-태평양 롱제비티 의학회(APLMS)는 싱가포르, 중국, 인도를 독립된 환경으로 활용하여 건강한 롱제비티를 일상생활로 확장하는 지역 모델을 개발 중입니다. 포스트 SCI 모델은
bodyKo: APLMS는 싱가포르, 중국, 인도를 활용해 롱제비티 과학이 기능, 예방, 그리고 대규모 건강한 삶으로 어떻게 이어질 수 있는지 시험할 예정입니다.

아시아-태평양 롱제비티 의학회(APLMS)는 싱가포르, 중국, 인도를 각각 실제 증거를 생성하고 예방 접근법을 시험하는 독립된 환경으로 활용하여 건강한 롱제비티를 일상생활로 확장하는 지역 모델을 개발 중입니다. 이 계획의 범위는 상당하며, 세 나라를 합쳐 약 28억 명, 즉 전 세계 인구의 3분의 1 이상을 차지하지만, 인구 규모는 전체 제안의 일부에 불과합니다.

홍콩에서 이 모델의 공개 데뷔가 이루어집니다: APLMS는 2026년 아시아-태평양 건강롱제비티 국제 정상회의(10월 1일부터 4일까지 열림)에서 SCI를 소개하고 더욱 발전시킬 예정입니다. 논의 중인 질문들은 겉보기에는 단순합니다 – 문화와 의료 시스템을 넘나드는 것, 현지에서 재창조해야 할 것, 그리고 이 모든 것이 실험실이나 전문 클리닉을 떠난 후 실제로 결과를 바꿀 수 있는지.

롱제비티. 기술: 롱제비티 의학은 노화 측정에 점점 더 정교해졌다; 더 중요한 시험은 이러한 측정이 더 많은 기능, 독립성, 회복력을 가진 삶으로 이어지는지, 그리고 만성 질환에 시달리는 기간이 줄어들지에 대한 것이다. 바이오마커는 노화 생물학에 대해 흥미로운 것을 알려줄 수 있다; 하지만 쇼핑을 위층으로 가져다줄 수는 없다. SCI 모델이 매우 다른 인구에 걸쳐 실제 증거를 강조하는 점은 특히 기술을 종착지가 아닌 수단으로 다루기 때문에 흥미롭다. 프리미엄 클리닉에만 국한된 롱제비티 의학은 결국 부유층의 취미에 불과하며, 인구 건강 전략이 아니다; 유용한 개입이 일반 의료, 직장, 지역사회에 도입되지 않으면 별로 중요하지 않다. 싱가포르, 중국, 인도에서는 그 여정이 다르게 보이며, 그렇지 않다고 가정하는 — 한 집단에서 효과가 다른 집단에 깔끔하게 전달될 것이라고 가정하는 것은 SCI가 시험하기 위해 만들어진 전제다. 산수만으로도 마음을 집중시켜야 한다: 약 28억 명의 인구 규모에서는 기능적 건강의 소소한 향상조차도 결코 미미하지 않는다. 흥미로운 질문은 그것들이 입증되고 — 그리고 실현될 수 있느냐 하는 것이다.

이러한 사고방식은 블루존, 즉 사람들이 유난히 나이를 잘 드는 지역에서 어느 정도 빚지고 있습니다. APLMS의 설명에 따르면, 많은 블루존에서 눈에 띄는 점은 특별한 것이 없다는 것입니다. 특별한 부도, 첨단 의료도 없이, 단지 평범한 사람들이 수십 년에 걸쳐 쌓아온 강한 일상 습관, 사회적 유대, 문화적 연속성 속에서 평범한 삶을 살아가는 것입니다. 이 패턴이 일반화되는지는 SCI가 가정하기보다는 검증하려는 바로 질문입니다.
APLMS는 싱가포르, 중국, 인도를 선택한 이유가 바로 이들이 상호 교환 가능하지 않기 때문입니다. 싱가포르는 확립된 공중보건 인프라와 인구 기반 의료를 노인과학 및 정밀 의학 연구와 결합하고 있습니다; 다문화 인구와 예방에 대한 강조는 롱제비티 접근법을 실천에서 평가할 수 있는 한 가지 환경을 제공합니다.
중국은 세계에서 두 번째로 큰 경제 대국으로, 14억 명이 넘는 인구를 보유하고 있으며, 디지털 헬스 역량 증가와 인구 건강 분야의 폭넓은 경험을 더해 다른 차원의 규모를 제공합니다. 중국의 의료 환경은 현대 의학과 오랜 문화적 전통을 모두 포함하여, 과학적 증거가 기존 행동과 치료 체계와 만날 때 번역이 무엇을 의미하는지 또 다른 시험대를 제공합니다.
현재 세계에서 인구가 가장 많은 인도는 식단, 문화, 가족 구조, 공동체 생활 면에서 상당한 이질성을 더하고 있습니다. APLMS는 또한 아유르베다와 그 일상 루틴, 영양, 수면, 신체 활동, 정신 건강에 대한 강조를 강조합니다; 이러한 전통들은 제안된 모델 내에서 인도의 과학, 의료 및 디지털 건강 역량 발전과 함께 공존할 것입니다.
의도는 롱제비티를 위한 단일 문화적 레시피를 찾는 것이 아닙니다. 오히려 반대입니다: SCI는 전이 가능한 원칙과 완강히 지역에만 머무는 원칙을 분리할 수 있는 증거 중심의 번역 네트워크로 구상됩니다.
이 모델의 핵심은 대체 측정에서 기능으로의 강조 전환입니다. 노화된 생물학과 바이오마커는 여전히 중요하며, 디지털 도구와 신흥 개입도 마찬가지입니다; 그러나 APLMS는 이러한 가치는 궁극적으로 이동성, 독립성, 만성 질환 부담, 웰빙, 장애 없는 시기와 비교해 평가되어야 한다고 주장합니다.
그 구분은 중요합니다. 롱제비티 연구는 점점 더 세밀한 생물학적 과정을 측정할 수 있게 되었지만, 바이오마커의 통계적으로 흥미로운 움직임이 반드시 임상적으로 의미 있는 이익을 가져오지는 않습니다. 기능은 더 복잡합니다. 또한 무시하기도 어렵습니다.
따라서 SCI는 임상 진료 과정에서 일어나는 일을 넘어 수십 년에 걸쳐 축적된 조건들—물론 식습관과 움직임뿐 아니라 사회적 연결, 환경, 목적, 지역사회 참여, 예방 치료 접근성—에도 관심을 보입니다. 의학과 기술은 이러한 기초를 이해하고 측정하며 강화하는 도구로 자리매김하며, 대체물이 아닙니다.
실제 증거 요소에서 모델이 더 야심차게 됩니다. 통제된 연구는 효능과 안전성을 입증하는 데 필수적이지만, 인구 건강은 다양한 식단, 의료 인프라, 사회경제적 상황, 문화적 기대 등 통제되지 않은 환경에서 이루어지는 불편한 경향이 있습니다.
APLMS는 SCI 건강한 롱제비티 실세계 근거 및 번역 네트워크를 구축할 계획이며, 2026–27년 초기 작업은 공유 프레임워크와 실용적 공통 결과, 그리고 실제 연구 기회, 임상가 교육, 실행 경로 제공을 포함할 예정입니다.

홍콩 정상회의에서 열리는 전용 세션인 'SCI 건강한 롱제비티 모델: 일상생활, 실제 증거 및 대규모 예방'이 이 과정을 시작하며, 연구자, 임상의, 의료 리더 및 실행 파트너를 한자리에 모을 것입니다. 과제는 연구 결과를 유용하게 만들기 위해 충분한 방법론적 일관성을 유지하면서도, 지역적 유연성을 충분히 허용해 관련성을 높이는 것입니다 – 맥락 없는 규모는 완전한 규모가 아닙니다.
아마도 더 큰 제안이 SCI가 궁극적으로 연구 결과를 향하도록 의도하는 방향일 것입니다. APLMS는 프리미엄 롱제비티 클리닉과 웰니스 서비스를 넘어 지역사회, 직장, 고용주, 보험사 및 기존 보건 시스템으로 근거 기반 접근법을 확장하는 경로를 명확히 구상합니다.
이는 이미 참여하는 롱제비티 소비자에게 또 다른 검사나 개입을 제공하는 것보다 훨씬 더 어려운 번역 문제입니다. 인구 수준에서의 예방은 접근성, 준수, 문화적 수용성, 의료 경제성과 경쟁해야 하며; 생물학적으로 그럴듯한 것이 실질적으로 사용 가능해져야 합니다.

APLMS 회장 팀 시 박사도 이 목표를 비슷한 방식으로 제시합니다. 그는 이 모델이 또 다른 이론적 틀을 만들거나 노화에 대한 단일 공식을 찾으려는 것이 아니라고 말했습니다; 그 목적은 "실용적이고 문화적으로 관련성 있으며 과학적으로 신뢰할 수 있고 확장 가능한 모델을 구축하고, 실제 세계의 증거를 통해 검증되어 더 나은 예방, 더 건강한 일상생활, 궁극적으로 더 나은 건강 결과로 전환하는 것"이라고 말했습니다.
그런 의미에서 아시아 태평양은 그 작업을 시도하기에 이례적으로 큰 무대를 제공한다 – 다양하고 빠르게 고화되고 있으며 너무 이질적이어서 쉽게 답하기 어렵다.
만약 SCI가 의도한 대로 발달한다면, 그 가치는 건강한 롱제비티의 또 다른 정의를 만드는 데 있기보다는, 수십억 명의 복잡하고 평범한 삶에 노출되었을 때 어떤 아이디어가 여전히 유용한지 발견하는 데 있을 수 있습니다. 결국 예방이 반드시 작동해야 할 부분이 바로 그 부분입니다.
2026년 아시아-태평양 건강롱제비티 국제 정상회의는 2026년 10월 1일부터 4일까지 홍콩 호프웰 호텔에서 열립니다 – 자세한 내용은 여기를 클릭하세요.
"SCI 모델이 임상을 넘어 롱제비티를 넘어 롱제비티"라는 글이 처음 게재되었습니다. 기술.

bodyOriginal.text: Outer Bio’s Yuna platform keeps living human skin functioning for a month, a longer window for testing what actually slows visible aging.

Cut a piece of human skin out of the body, and the clock starts ticking. Within days, it stops behaving like skin at all. The cells that once fought inflammation, rebuilt collagen and healed wounds start to shut down. For the scientists trying to figure out which compounds actually slow skin aging, that short window has always been the problem. You can’t watch a process that takes weeks to unfold if your test tissue is dead before week one even ends.

A new company thinks it has cracked that particular puzzle. Outer Bio came out of stealth this week with a platform called Yuna, which keeps full-thickness human skin (epidermis, dermis, immune cells and all) alive and testable for a full four weeks [ 1 ]. That’s long enough, the company says, to watch the slow biological processes behind aging skin actually happen in real time, in real human tissue.

Skincare is a more than $100 billion industry, and yet in three decades of research, only one topical ingredient (here’s looking at you, retinoids) has earned FDA recognition for visibly improving aging skin.

Outer Bio’s pitch is that this isn’t for lack of trying or lack of money. It’s a technical bottleneck. The biology that matters for aging skin – how collagen rebuilds itself, how chronic low-grade inflammation (“inflammaging,” as longevity researchers have taken to calling it) does its damage, how senescent cells pile up and stop functioning – takes weeks to play out. Standard lab skin can’t survive that long, so researchers have effectively been asked to judge a marathon by watching the first hundred yards.

Yuna is built to remove that constraint. The tissue comes from donors spanning different ages, sexes, and skin tones, and it’s tracked continuously for the full month. Cell activity, tissue structure and protein signals. Each compound tested generates more than 30,000 data points, and the company says it has already amassed over 10 terabytes of data from more than 300 donors and 10,000 individual treatments.

The living-tissue data is designed to feed a machine-learning system that gets smarter with every test. Models trained on Yuna’s results help prioritize which compounds to try next, and each new result sharpens the next prediction. Outer Bio says its virtual screening library already covers 5.9 million compounds, with plans to eventually work through libraries in the billions.

“Skincare has never lacked demand or ambition. It has lacked the ability to study compounds and mechanisms in living human skin over a biologically relevant timeframe,” said Michael Polansky, co-founder and CEO of Outer Bio. “Most experimental platforms rely on reconstructed skin or cell monolayers. Those models can tell you whether a compound is toxic; they can’t tell you whether it works, because they lack the complexity and architecture of the real organ. And they fail within days, before the biology that matters even begins. We built Yuna to close that gap.”

The company has backed up that claim with public data. A preprint posted to bioRxiv documents Yuna reproducing three known skin conditions across the full four-week window, sustained psoriasis-like inflammation that responded to a JAK inhibitor, senescence markers in aged donor tissue that dropped after a senolytic treatment and UV damage that a topical sunscreen measurably reduced. None of those outcomes, Outer Bio argues, would have shown up in a shorter-lived model.
A longevity tool wearing a skincare label

It’s easy to file this under beauty industry news and move on. However, the underlying idea (senescent cells accumulating, inflammation quietly compounding, tissue losing its ability to repair itself) is the same biology longevity researchers chase in every other organ in the body. Skin just happens to be the one organ scientists can study without surgery, which makes it a useful proving ground for aging science more broadly.

If a platform like Yuna can reliably show that a senolytic combination reverses senescence markers in living tissue, that’s a data point for aging research well beyond what shows up on a store shelf. Outer Bio is opening the platform to select biopharma and ingredient partners, meaning its four-week window may end up informing therapeutics as much as it does the next serum.

articles.titleKo: 아우터 바이오는 과학자들에게 노화 피부를 연구할 한 달을 제공합니다
articles.summaryKo: 아우터 바이오의 유나 플랫폼은 한 달 동안 살아있는 인간 피부가 기능하도록 유지하며, 이는 실제로 눈에 띄는 노화를 늦추는 요인을 테스트할 수 있는 더 긴 기간입니다. 몸에서 인간 피부 한 조각을 잘라내면 시간이 흐르기 시작합니다. 며칠 만에 피부처럼 전혀 행동하지 않습니다. 한때 염증과 싸우고 콜라겐을 재구성하며 [...] 아우터 바이오가 과학자들에게 노화 피부를 연구할 한 달을 제공했다는 글이 나왔습니다
bodyKo: 아우터 바이오의 유나 플랫폼은 한 달 동안 인간의 피부 기능을 유지하며, 이는 실제로 눈에 띄는 노화를 늦추는 요인을 테스트할 수 있는 더 긴 기간입니다.

몸에서 인간 피부 한 조각을 잘라내면 시간이 흐르기 시작합니다. 며칠 만에 피부처럼 전혀 행동하지 않습니다. 염증과 싸우고, 콜라겐을 재구성하며, 상처를 치유했던 세포들이 점차 기능을 멈추기 시작합니다. 어떤 화합물이 실제로 피부 노화를 늦추는지 알아내려는 과학자들에게 그 짧은 시간이 항상 문제였습니다. 검사 조직이 1주 차도 채 지나지 않고 죽었다면, 몇 주가 걸리는 과정을 지켜볼 수 없습니다.
새로운 회사는 그 수수께끼를 풀었다고 생각한다. Outer Bio는 이번 주에 Yuna라는 플랫폼을 은밀하게 출시했는데, 이 플랫폼은 인간의 피부(표피, 진피, 면역 세포 포함)를 4주 동안 살아 있고 검사 가능하게 유지한다 [1]. 회사는 이 정도면 노화 피부 뒤에 있는 느린 생물학적 과정을 실제 인간 조직에서 실시간으로 관찰하기에 충분하다고 말한다.
스킨케어는 1,000억 달러가 넘는 산업이지만, 30년에 걸친 연구 끝에 단 하나의 국소 성분(여기 레티노이드)만이 노화 피부를 눈에 띄게 개선한다는 이유로 FDA로부터 인정을 받았습니다.

아우터 바이오의 주장은 이것이 시도 부족이나 자금 부족 때문이 아니라는 것이다. 이것은 기술적인 병목 현상이다. 노화 피부에 중요한 생물학 – 콜라겐이 어떻게 재건되는지, 만성 저등급 염증('인플램징'이라고 롱제비티 연구자들이 부르는 표현)이 어떻게 손상을 일으키는지, 노쇠한 세포가 어떻게 쌓여 기능을 멈추는지는 몇 주가 걸린다. 표준 실험실 피부는 그렇게 오래 버틸 수 없기 때문에, 연구자들은 사실상 마라톤을 처음 100야드만 관찰하며 판단해야 한다.

Yuna는 이러한 제약을 없애도록 설계되었습니다. 조직은 다양한 연령, 성별, 피부색을 가진 기증자들로부터 나오며, 한 달 내내 지속적으로 추적됩니다. Cell 활성, 조직 구조, 단백질 신호. 각 검사 화합물은 30,000개 이상의 데이터 포인트를 생성하며, 회사는 이미 300명 이상의 기증자와 10,000건의 개별 치료에서 10테라바이트 이상의 데이터를 수집했다고 밝혔습니다.

이 생체 조직 데이터는 매 테스트마다 점점 더 똑똑해지는 머신러닝 시스템에 공급되도록 설계되었습니다. 유나의 결과를 기반으로 학습된 모델은 다음에 어떤 화합물을 우선순위를 정하고, 새로운 결과가 나올 때마다 예측이 더욱 날카로워집니다. 아우터 바이오는 가상 스크리닝 라이브러리가 이미 590만 개의 화합물을 커버하고 있으며, 앞으로 수십억 개의 라이브러리를 통해 연구할 계획이라고 밝혔습니다.

"스킨케어는 수요나 야망이 부족한 적이 없습니다. 생물학적으로 중요한 시간 동안 살아있는 인간 피부의 화합물과 메커니즘을 연구할 능력이 부족했습니다,"라고 아우터 바이오의 공동 창립자이자 CEO인 마이클 폴란스키가 말했습니다. "대부분의 실험 플랫폼은 재구성된 피부나 세포 단층에 의존합니다. 그 모델들은 화합물이 독성인지 알려줄 수 있지만; 실제 장기의 복잡성과 구조가 부족하기 때문에 효과가 있는지는 알 수 없습니다. 그리고 중요한 생물학이 시작되기 전 며칠 내에 실패합니다. 우리는 그 격차를 메우기 위해 유나를 만들었습니다."

이 회사는 공개 데이터로 이 주장을 뒷받침했다. bioRxiv에 게시된 프리프린트에는 유나가 4주 전체 기간 동안 세 가지 알려진 피부 질환을 재현한 내용이 기록되어 있다. JAK 억제제에 반응한 지속적인 건선 유사 염증, 세놀리틱 치료 후 노화된 기증자 조직의 노화세포 마커, 그리고 국소 자외선 차단제로 측정 가능한 자외선 손상을 측정한 결과이다. 아우터 바이오는 이러한 결과들 중 어느 것도 단수명 모델에서는 나타나지 않았을 것이라고 주장한다.
스킨케어 라벨을 붙인 롱제비티 도구
이것을 미용 산업 뉴스로 분류하고 넘어가기 쉽습니다. 하지만 근본적인 개념(노화 세포 축적, 염증 조용히 복합, 조직 스스로 회복 능력 상실)은 롱제비티 연구자들이 신체의 다른 모든 장기에서 쫓는 동일한 생물학적 원리입니다. 피부는 과학자들이 수술 없이도 연구할 수 있는 유일한 장기로, 노화 과학 전반에 유용한 시험장이 됩니다.

Yuna와 같은 플랫폼이 세놀리틱 조합이 살아있는 조직의 노화세포 마커를 되돌린다는 것을 신뢰성 있게 입증한다면, 이는 노화 연구에 있어 매장 진열대에 나오는 것보다 훨씬 더 큰 데이터 포인트가 될 것입니다. Outer Bio는 바이오제약 및 성분 파트너를 선정하여 플랫폼을 개방하고 있어, 4주 기간이 다음 세럼만큼이나 치료제에도 영향을 미칠 수 있습니다.
[1] https://www.outerbio.com/news/outer-bio-emerges-from-stealth-with-yuna-a-platform-that-keeps-ex-vivo-human-skin-alive-and-measurable-for-four-weeks
"아우터 바이오가 과학자들에게 노화 피부를 연구할 한 달 시간을 제공한다"는 글이 롱제비티에 처음 게재되었습니다. 기술.

articles.titleOriginal: Retro Biosciences tweaks its Alzheimer’s pill dosing
articles.summaryOriginal: Sam Altman-backed Retro Biosciences is widening its Alzheimer’s trial after early doses showed no red flags. Most drug trials pray for a boring readout. Retro Biosciences got exactly that, and now it has a problem precisely because nothing went wrong. bodyOriginal.text: Sam Altman-backed Retro Biosciences is widening its Alzheimer’s trial after early doses showed no red flags .
Most drug trials pray for a boring readout. Retro Biosciences got exactly that, and now it has a problem precisely because nothing went wrong.

The Sam Altman-funded longevity startup is testing a pill called RTR-242, designed to help the brain clear out cellular junk that piles up with age and is thought to worsen conditions like Alzheimer’s and Parkinson’s [ 1 ].

According to Retro CEO Joe Betts-LaCroix, the drug’s early safety data has been almost suspiciously clean: no major side effects, no safety signals, nothing. Betts-LaCroix told Business Insider that’s a mixed blessing. Without any signal at all, it’s hard to know whether the drug is actually doing anything, or simply not doing enough.

So Retro is upping the dose and the headcount. The company is adding two new cohorts to its Phase 1 safety trial, expanding total enrollment by more than 42%, from 76 to 108 participants. The hope, somewhat counterintuitively, is to see something.
“Hopefully, at some point, we will at least get headaches or something,” Betts-LaCroix said, only half-joking about the search for a dose potent enough to matter without becoming unsafe.
Joe Betts-LaCroix is founder and CEO of Retro Biosciences.

RTR-242 targets lysosomes, the recycling centers inside every cell that break down old, damaged proteins so the cell can reuse the parts. That recycling process, called autophagy, tends to slow down with age, and researchers increasingly view a sluggish cleanup system as one of the threads connecting general aging to specific neurodegenerative diseases. Retro’s drug is designed to restore the acidity that aging lysosomes lose, essentially sharpening a dulled tool rather than replacing it.

Retro isn’t alone in betting on this mechanism. Boston-based Lysoway Therapeutics began its own first-in-human trial targeting lysosomes in May, backed in part by the Michael J Fox Foundation. That same month, Chicago’s Vanqua Bio reported promising early safety results from a similar approach aimed at Parkinson’s. It’s a crowded corner of neuroscience, but crowded doesn’t mean solved; nobody has yet proven a lysosome-targeting drug works in patients.

Paul Robbins, a biochemist and longevity researcher at the University of Minnesota who isn’t involved in the Retro trial, called the lysosome an “interesting target,” particularly for cognitive decline. He said he’s encouraged by the lack of toxicity so far, but wants to see more before celebrating.

“If they’re not seeing toxicity, that’s great,” Robbins said, adding that he doesn’t yet know exactly how the drug works or whether it will help people who actually have dementia, since RTR-242 is currently being tested only in healthy volunteers ages 18 to 65.
For Betts-LaCroix, the project isn’t abstract. He lost his father to Alzheimer’s earlier this year.
“You make it into your 90s and then, damn. It comes along and strips your personhood out right from under you,” he said.

That’s really the pitch behind the whole longevity category Retro competes in: not immortality, but more good years, and fewer of them lost to diseases that erase who a person is before the body gives out.

Retro Biosciences says its broader mission is adding ten healthy years to the human lifespan, and RTR-242 is its most concrete swing at that goal so far. Rivals like Altos Labs and New Limit are working on their own approaches to aging biology, but as of now, neither has announced a drug in human trials, which puts Retro, for the moment, a step ahead in the race to find the first genuine longevity drug. Whether that lead holds may come down to something as unglamorous as finding the right dose.
[1] https://www.businessinsider.com/retro-biotech-testing-higher-doses-of-rtr-242-alzheimers-drug-2026-8

articles.titleKo: 레트로 바이오사이언스가 알츠하이머 약 용량을 조정하다
articles.summaryKo: 샘 알트만이 지원하는 레트로 바이오사이언스는 초기 투여에서 아무런 경고 신호가 없어 알츠하이머 임상시험을 확대하고 있다. 대부분의 약물 임상시험은 지루한 결과만 나오길 바란다. 레트로 바이오사이언스는 바로 그런 결과를 얻었고, 아무 문제도 없었기 때문에 이제 문제가 생겼다. 샘 알트만이 자금을 지원하는 롱제비티 스타트업은 RTR-242라는 알약을 시험하고 있으며, 이는 [...] 레트로 바이오사이언스가 알츠하이머를 약간 조정하다
bodyKo: 샘 알트만이 지원하는 레트로 바이오사이언스는 초기 접종 결과에 이상 징후가 없어 알츠하이머 임상시험을 확대하고 있습니다.
대부분의 신약 임상시험은 지루한 결과만 나오길 바란다. 레트로 바이오사이언스는 바로 그 결과를 얻었고, 아무 문제도 없었기 때문에 문제가 생겼다.
샘 알트만이 자금을 지원하는 롱제비티 스타트업은 RTR-242라는 알약을 시험 중인데, 이 약은 나이가 들면서 쌓이는 세포 정체를 제거하도록 돕기 위해 고안되었으며, 알츠하이머병과 파킨슨병 같은 질환을 악화시키는 것으로 여겨집니다 [1].

Retro CEO 조 베츠-라크루아에 따르면, 이 약물의 초기 안전성 데이터는 거의 의심스러울 정도로 깨끗했습니다: 주요 부작용도 없고, 안전 신호도 없으며, 아무것도 없습니다. 베츠-라크루아는 비즈니스 인사이더와의 인터뷰에서 이것이 복합된 축복이라고 말했습니다. 전혀 신호가 없으면 약물이 실제로 효과가 있는지, 아니면 단순히 충분히 효과가 없는지 알기 어렵습니다.
그래서 레트로는 용량과 인원을 늘리고 있습니다. 회사는 1상 안전성 시험에 두 명의 새로운 코호트를 추가하여 총 등록 인원을 76명에서 108명으로 42% 이상 늘렸습니다. 다소 직관에 반하는 희망은 무언가를 보는 것입니다.
"언젠가는 적어도 두통이나 그런 일이 생길 거야," 베츠-라크루아가 말했다. 위험하지 않으면서도 의미 있을 만큼 강력한 용량을 찾는 과정에 대해 반쯤 농담 섞인 듯했다.
조 베츠-라크루아는 Retro Biosciences의 창립자이자 CEO입니다.

RTR-242는 모든 세포 내부의 재활용 센터인 라이소좀을 표적으로 삼는데, 이 센터는 오래되고 손상된 단백질을 분해해 세포가 그 부품을 재사용할 수 있게 합니다. 이 재활용 과정인 자가포식은 나이가 들수록 느려지는 경향이 있으며, 연구자들은 점점 느린 정화 시스템을 일반적인 노화와 특정 신경퇴행성 질환을 연결하는 실마리 중 하나로 보고 있습니다. 레트로의 약물은 노화 리소좀이 잃는 산도를 회복하도록 설계되어, 본질적으로 무뎌진 도구를 교체하는 것이 아니라 연마시키는 것입니다.

레트로만 이 메커니즘에 베팅하는 것은 아닙니다. 보스턴에 본사를 둔 라이소웨이 테라퓨틱스는 마이클 J 폭스 재단의 일부 지원을 받아 5월에 라이소좀을 대상으로 한 최초의 인간 대상 임상시험을 시작했습니다. 같은 달, 시카고의 반콰 바이오는 파킨슨병을 겨냥한 유사한 접근법에서 유망한 초기 안전성 결과를 보고했습니다. 신경과학 분야에서 경쟁이 치열한 분야이지만, 혼잡하다고 해서 해결된 것은 아닙니다; 아직 아무도 환자에게 리소좀 표적 약물이 효과가 있음을 증명하지 않았습니다.
미네소타 대학교의 생화학자이자 롱제비티 연구자인 폴 로빈스는 리소좀을 특히 인지 저하에 있어 "흥미로운 표적"이라고 평가했습니다. 그는 지금까지 독성이 없다는 점에 고무적이지만, 축하하기 전에 더 많은 결과를 보고 싶다고 말했습니다.
"독성이 없다면 다행입니다,"라고 로빈스는 말하며, 현재 RTR-242가 18세에서 65세 사이의 건강한 자원자에게만 시험되고 있어 약물이 정확히 어떻게 작용하는지, 실제 치매 환자에게 도움이 될지 아직 알지 못한다고 덧붙였습니다.
베츠-라크루아에게 이 프로젝트는 추상적이지 않습니다. 그는 올해 초 알츠하이머로 아버지를 잃었습니다.
"90대가 되어서, 젠장. 그게 와서 네 인격을 완전히 빼앗아가게 해," 그가 말했다.
이것이 바로 레트로가 경쟁하는 롱제비티 장수 카테고리의 핵심입니다: 불멸이 아니라, 더 많은 좋은 해를 보내고, 몸이 고장 나기 전에 사람을 지워버리는 질병으로 잃는 시간이 적다는 것입니다.

레트로 바이오사이언스는 인간의 건강한 수명을 10년을 늘리는 것이 더 넓은 목표라고 밝혔으며, RTR-242는 지금까지 그 목표에 가장 구체적인 변화입니다. Altos Labs와 New Limit 같은 경쟁사들은 노화 생물학에 대한 독자적인 접근법을 개발 중이지만, 현재까지 두 곳 모두 인간 임상시험에서 약물을 발표하지 않아 레트로가 최초의 진정한 롱제비티 약물을 찾는 경쟁에서 한 발 앞서 나가고 있음을 의미합니다. 그 선두가 유지될지는 적절한 용량을 찾는 것과 같은 화려하지 않은 문제일 수 있습니다.
[1] https://www.businessinsider.com/retro-biotech-testing-higher-doses-of-rtr-242-alzheimers-drug-2026-8
레트로 바이오사이언스가 알츠하이머 알츠하이머 약 용량을 조정하다 보도, 이 글은 롱제비티에 처음 게재되었습니다. 기술.

articles.titleOriginal: Your Personal Longevity Assistant: Evipedia Grok Bot
articles.summaryOriginal: With Grok Bot, SpaceXAi has created something really special and helpful. And the Evipedia Grok Bot turns this gem into something even more […]

bodyOriginal.text: With Grok Bot , SpaceXAi has created something really special and helpful. And the Evipedia Grok Bot turns this gem into something even more precious. A specialized AI assistant offering an evidence-based 2nd opinion on health and longevity interventions.
It integrates Grok, the AI4L persona , the Evipedia MCP server , and Evipedia-hosted search into one super-useful companion.

What Evipedia Grok Bot will do for you The bot will allow you to have interactive conversations about a wide range of health and longevity interventions. It delivers helpful 2nd opinions on these topics, and all its answers are grounded in the same principles and behavior used by Evipedia and AI4L:

Tailored for the Longevity Community — answers are framed for risk-aware adults actively optimizing their health, not for the general population Evidence First — conclusions rest on human clinical trials and meta-analyses; conflicting, thin, or absent evidence is named as such rather than smoothed over Graded Findings — each benefit and risk carries an explicit High, Medium, Low, or Speculative grade and, where the literature supports one, a magnitude The Full Picture — interventions are looked at across mechanism, benefits, risks, interactions, protocol, monitoring, and open research Commercial Interests — when the evidence comes from parties with a financial stake in the intervention, or from an organization whose members profit from the position it endorses, conflicts are named on every side of the debate Evipedia Lookup — health and longevity questions are checked against the evidence reviews on evipedia.ai before the model answers from memory Plain Language — acronyms and jargon get a short explanation at first use, and scientific nomenclature follows field convention Verified Links — every PMID, NCT ID, and DOI is retrieved and checked before it is shown; a URL that cannot be verified is omitted rather than guessed Review Suggestions — when an intervention under sustained discussion has no Evipedia review, the model offers to suggest it to the Evipedia editorial team or points to generating an evidence review using the AI4L prompt What’s in Evipedia Evipedia is a comprehensive, continuously updated online encyclopedia that provides much-needed, accurate, and up-to-date information on a wide range of health and longevity-related interventions.

Free to Use — Evipedia is completely free to use and open to everyone. We built Evipedia as a backbone tool for the whole longevity and rejuvenation community. Our goal is to empower individuals with knowledge to make informed decisions about their health and longevity. 770+ Evidence Reviews — Including whole-body therapies, brain health, skin rejuvenation, hormone optimization, peptides, psychedelics, medications, blood and plasma therapies, complementary cancer approaches, foundational habits, diets, foods, probiotics, botanicals, isolates, and many more. A Dual Structure for Every Entry — Each intervention has a one-page Quick Reference Sheet for an at-a-glance protocol, benefits, risks, contraindications, and monitoring, plus a Full Evidence Review for in-depth analysis. Continuous Updates — Entries are continuously updated to reflect the latest developments in health and longevity. On average, reviews are refreshed every 4-6 weeks, ensuring access to the most current information available. Full Audit and Quality Transparency — Every “Quick Reference Sheet” and “Evidence Review” on Evipedia includes an Audit Report that outlines the detailed audit criteria and the history of audits and fixes applied to the documents. Stable Permalinks – Beautiful Sharing Cards — Every intervention has a fixed, short URL and a purpose-designed social sharing card — ideal for citing a compound in a supplement stack or anchoring a claim in an online discussion. AI & Agent-friendly, Extensive Integration Support — Built as a backbone service for the longevity and rejuvenation community, Evipedia features a wide variety of AI integration tools and an easily accessible API . All are free to use, under an AI- and agent-friendly site policy and the Creative Commons 4.0 license. Built on AI4L — Evipedia is built on top of our open-source AI4L framework , which enables anyone to create high-quality, evidence-based reviews of health and longevity interventions. At the core of AI4L is our novel “ Audit-Driven Prompting ” approach to generate hallucination-free, accurate, and well-structured reviews using frontier AI models. articles.titleOriginal: From World Cup Champions to Longevity Champions
articles.summaryOriginal: Fresh from Spain’s spectacular victory in the 2026 FIFA World Cup, Madrid is preparing for another kind of world-class gathering: one focused not on winning more years of sporting glory, but on […]

bodyOriginal.text: Fresh from Spain’s spectacular victory in the 2026 FIFA World Cup, Madrid is preparing for another kind of world-class gathering: one focused not on winning more years of sporting glory, but on winning more healthy years of life.

On September 30 and October 1, 2026, the International Longevity Summit Madrid 2026 will bring together leading scientists, physicians, entrepreneurs, investors and futurists to explore one of humanity’s greatest challenges—and potentially greatest opportunities: extending healthy human life.

Organized by the International Longevity Alliance, the Summit comes to a city uniquely positioned to lead the global conversation on longevity. Spain has the highest life expectancy in the European Union, while the Comunidad de Madrid has recorded the highest life expectancy of any EU region, reaching the remarkable landmark of 85.7 years according to Eurostat. Madrid may therefore be more than simply a great European capital; it could increasingly be considered a “Blue Zone 2.0”: a modern, dynamic metropolis where exceptional longevity meets cutting-edge science, biotechnology and innovation.

bodyOriginal.alt: LSM 2

bodyOriginal.text: And now, after Spain’s national team, La Roja, captured the 2026 FIFA World Cup, Spain can proudly claim another world-leading achievement. In July, Spain defeated Argentina 1–0 after extra time to win its second men’s World Cup title, adding a new chapter to a country already renowned for its health, lifestyle and longevity.

From world champions on the football field to potential champions of healthy longevity, Spain is demonstrating that the future may belong to those who know how to live—and perhaps someday live much longer.

bodyOriginal.alt: LSM 3

bodyOriginal.text: A new royal home at Spain’s most prestigious medical institution After the success of previous editions held at the Ilustre Colegio Oficial de Médicos de Madrid (ICOMEM), where the Summit was inaugurated with the participation of the Mayor of Madrid, José Luis Martínez-Almeida, the 2026 edition takes a major institutional step forward.

This year, the Summit will be held at the magnificent Real Academia Nacional de Medicina de España (RANME), the Royal National Academy of Medicine of Spain, the country’s most prestigious medical institution. Founded in 1734, the Academy occupies a unique place in Spanish scientific history. The Academy is under the High Patronage of His Majesty King Felipe VI, underlining the exceptional institutional importance of the venue. The Academy is also historically associated with some of the greatest names in medicine, including Spain’s Nobel laureates Santiago Ramón y Cajal and Severo Ochoa.

Located in the historic heart of Madrid, between the Royal Palace and the Teatro Real, the RANME will provide an extraordinary setting for a conversation that could reshape the future of medicine itself.

From George Church and Ray Kurzweil to Eric Topol and Peter Diamandis The International Longevity Summit has rapidly become a meeting point for some of the world’s most influential thinkers in longevity, biotechnology, medicine and the future of humanity.

Previous editions of the International Longevity Summit in Madrid have featured an exceptional roster of speakers, including George Church , pioneering geneticist; Ray Kurzweil , futurist and inventor; Steve Horvath , creator of the epigenetic clock; Andrea Maier , longevity physician and researcher; Mehmood Khan , global health and life sciences leader; Liz Parrish , biotechnology entrepreneur; Aubrey de Grey , biomedical gerontologist; Bryan Johnson , entrepreneur and longevity pioneer; María Blasco , molecular biologist and telomere researcher; João Pedro de Magalhães , biogerontologist and aging researcher; and Michael Ringel , biotechnology and pharmaceutical executive—along with many other leading scientists, physicians, entrepreneurs, and innovators from around the world.

The 2026 edition continues and expands this tradition of quality. Among the distinguished participants and speakers announced for 2026 are Eric Topol , cardiologist and digital medicine pioneer; Peter Diamandis , entrepreneur and futurist; Brian Kennedy , aging researcher; Valentin Fuster , cardiologist and cardiovascular scientist; Bashayer Almubarak , longevity and health innovation leader; Guido Kroemer , cell biologist and aging researcher; Steven Austad , biogerontologist; Michel Poulain , demographer and Blue Zones researcher; Michael West , stem cell pioneer; Mike Chan , longevity expert and entrepreneur; Wei-Wu He , biotechnology entrepreneur; Patrick E. Sewell , longevity physician; Ronald Bonilla , dentist and longevity innovator; Tina Woods , health and longevity leader; Daniel Wallerstorfer , geneticist and biotech entrepreneur; David Wood , futurist and longevity advocate; and Kenneth Scott , entrepreneur and longevity advocate—along with many other leading international and Spanish scientists, physicians, entrepreneurs, and innovators.

The program will span the biology of aging, rejuvenation biotechnology, preventive and regenerative medicine, artificial intelligence, health data, biomarkers, the longevity economy and the profound social consequences of potentially dramatic increases in human healthspan.

From conference to scientific marketplace: posters and startup pitches debut in 2026 For the first time, the International Longevity Summit will introduce scientific poster sessions and startup pitches, opening the stage to a new generation of researchers, entrepreneurs and innovators. Through an international Open Call, selected participants will have the opportunity to present research projects, scientific posters, short talks and startup initiatives to an audience of experts, investors, physicians and longevity enthusiasts. The goal is to make the Summit not only a place where established leaders discuss the future, but also a platform where the next generation of breakthroughs, companies and scientific careers can begin.

A distinguished group of prestigious Spanish and international institutions is supporting this historic event, organized by International Longevity Alliance (ILA) at the Royal National Academy of Medicine of Spain (RANME) , in collaboration with the Official College of Physicians of Madrid (ICOMEM) and Madrid Innovation . International supporters include European Wellness and Triple Helix Science at the Gold level, as well as Novogenia and Nesa World at the Silver level. The event is also endorsed by leading foundations and organizations, including HealthGevity Nation, Hevolution Foundation, Human Longevity Inc., HumanityPlus, Immortalis, KHL Foundation, Life Extension Foundation, Lifeboat Foundation, Longevity Escape Velocity Foundation, Millennium Project, XPRIZE Foundation , together with innovative companies such as Cenegenics , GERO , and OXANA . This year, the Summit will also welcome a new generation of startups working in healthtech, healthcare innovation and longevity, with the logistical support of CRRATE and StartUp Olé Salamanca .
The 2026 edition aims to further strengthen Madrid’s role as a bridge between Europe, Latin America, North America and the rapidly expanding global longevity economy.

bodyOriginal.text: Two days of UNESCO history before exploring the future The Summit will begin even before the scientific program officially opens. On September 28 and 29, participants will be able to join two special pre-conference excursions to some of the most remarkable UNESCO World Heritage sites surrounding Madrid. The first day will travel south-east to Alcalá de Henares, Aranjuez and Toledo . The second will head north-west to Ávila, Segovia and El Escorial .

The contrast is intentional: participants will explore centuries of Spanish and European history before returning to Madrid to discuss technologies that may transform the future of human life itself. From ancient cathedrals and royal palaces to cellular rejuvenation, artificial intelligence and longevity escape velocity, the International Longevity Summit 2026 promises a journey through both humanity’s past and its possible future.

This summer, Spain has shown the world how to win on the football field. This autumn, Madrid will invite the world to explore how humanity might also win the greatest matches of all: the race against aging!

articles.titleOriginal: Calcium Mishandling Contributes to Muscle Loss
articles.summaryOriginal: Researchers have discovered and explained how calcium mishandling in muscle cells leads to long-term muscle weakness in older people. Calcium is not just for bones […]

bodyOriginal.text: Researchers have discovered and explained how calcium mishandling in muscle cells leads to long-term muscle weakness in older people .

Calcium is not just for bones Skeletal muscle cells use calcium ions to control how and when they contract. This activity is modulated by CaMKII, a protein kinase that also regulates muscle adaptations in response to exercise [1] and serves a great many unrelated functions throughout multiple other tissues.

In young tissues, this system works well, with exercise producing reactive oxygen species (ROS) that are used to stimulate muscle growth [1]. However, with aging, this falls apart in multiple ways: calcium ions leak out of where they are supposed to be [2], mitochondria and calcium become uncoupled [3], and, as has been well-known for decades, ROS and oxidative damage are no longer properly mitigated [4]. The authors hypothesized that CaMKII signaling is involved in this dysregulation.

Constant expression weakens muscles In their first experiment, the researchers examined the muscles of 3.7-month-old mice and compared them to those of 33-month-old mice; 33 months is exceptionally old for a mouse, and mice of that age were provided by the gerontologist Dr. Rafael deCabo. These elderly mice had significantly smaller muscles than the younger group, substantially more CaMKII in muscle tissue, and more evidence of CaMKII activity while at rest. However, the researchers noted that the biomarker they used to detect activity, pT287-CaMKII, is not entirely consistent in various muscle tissues and CaMKII can be modified in many other ways [5].

To determine the effects of constant CAMKII activity in muscle, this team developed a adeno-associated virus (AAV) that caused it to become active only in that tissue. This AAV had local effects, meaning that the researchers were able to inject it onto only one tibialis anterior muscle of each individual mouse; the identical muscle on the other side was injected with a simple fluorescent reporter protein with no significant effects. Interestingly, feedback mechanisms caused natural CAMKII to be suppressed in the muscles that were given this artificial CAMKII increase.

Within less than two months, this increase in constant CaMKII caused the targeted muscles to shrink and become pound-for-pound weaker than the unmodified muscles in the same mice; direct stimulation at multiple frequencies found that the targeted muscles were unable to exert nearly as much force. While it did not impact total mitochondrial number, it had significant negative effects on mitochondrial organization. A similar experiment with a different cohort of mice found that, after nine months, the loss of muscle mass became even more significant.

Some of this muscle loss was found to be driven by inflammation. Blocking the inflammatory signal NF-κB while activating CaMKII blunted some of the effects; the muscles in this group did not become pound-for-pound weaker, but they still lost mass.

Age-related gene expression changes Gene expression was also significantly impacted. While there were some differences, the impact of constant CaMKII expression was broadly similar to that of natural aging in muscle, and the researchers identified many biochemical pathways that are increased both by natural aging and by increased CaMKII. Most notably, iron-handling pathways were significantly disrupted by CaMKII.

The researchers also injected naturally aged mice with CN19o, which inhibits CaMKII; while individual genes were not significantly affected, the sum total of gene expression was found to move towards a more youthful phenotype. While it did not increase muscle size in 21-month-old mice, suppressing CaMKII in these mice increased their ability to contract.

The researchers hold that age-related constant CaMKII signaling is a significant contributor to sarcopenia. In youth, this signaling is beneficial, but in an aged environment, it is apparently doing more harm than good. However, the researchers did not experimentally validate why constant CaMKII activation has the mitochondrial effects it does, nor did they fully elucidate the connection between calcium and iron signaling. Further work will need to be done to determine if CaMKII is a useful target in people.
